clue.text: Was keeping Republican popular a dangerous thing in the main?

definitions.text: a dangerous thing in the main

explanation.surface: A question about whether backing a popular Republican was a dangerous move in the main race or contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The main' is the old poetic word for the open sea, so the definition is a cryptic description of a fighting ship, not a political risk.
explanation.definitionFit: A warship is a dangerous thing to meet on the high seas, the main.

clue.text: Pork pie with insect underneath

indicators.note: in a down entry the second piece is written underneath the first

parts.note: a hopper is a leaping insect such as a grasshopper

explanation.surface: A pork pie with a bug found lurking underneath it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pork pie' is Cockney rhyming slang for a lie (porky pie), and a whopper is a big lie. 'Underneath' places HOPPER below W in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A whopper is a blatant lie, which rhyming slang calls a pork pie.

clue.text: Fix section of armrest — or else!

indicators.note: the answer is a section cut from the run of letters that follows

explanation.surface: A menacing order to repair the broken part of a chair's armrest, or face the consequences.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash and 'or else!' make it read as a threat, which hides the word straddling three words.
explanation.definitionFit: To restore something is to fix it back to its former condition.

clue.text: Building hotel next to river

parts.note: H is Hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet
the Ouse is a river in England

explanation.surface: An estate agent's line about a building beside a hotel on the riverside.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ouse is one of several English rivers of that name, a setter's favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym by example: a home is the everyday kind of building the word names.

clue.text: Pert bust initially trembling under items of clothing — most fetching

indicators.note: in a down answer, under places the first letter of trembling below the ties
bust means broken, so the letters of Pert are smashed and rearranged

parts.note: ties are neckwear, items of clothing

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the first letter of trembling is used

explanation.surface: A cheeky bosom, quivering slightly beneath the outfit, is the most attractive sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' looks like part of the body but is the anagram signal: Pert becomes PRET. In a down clue, 'under' sets T beneath TIES.
explanation.definitionFit: Fetching means attractive, so the most fetching thing is the prettiest, a superlative synonym.

clue.text: Harry ultimately drives black and white diggers

parts.note: to harry someone is to badger them

indicators.note: take the final letter of drives

explanation.surface: Prince Harry, in the end, drives some black-and-white vehicles or animals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harry' reads as a name but is the verb meaning to pester.
explanation.definitionFit: Badgers are black-and-white striped animals that dig setts.

clue.text: Located a shilling in the sack

indicators.note: in means the pieces go inside the bed

parts.note: to hit the sack is to go to bed, so the sack is bed
s was the abbreviation for the old British shilling

explanation.surface: A shilling coin is found lying in a sack.
explanation.walkthrough: A shilling was an old British coin, written s. A and S go in BED.
explanation.definitionFit: Based means located somewhere, as in a firm based in Leeds.

clue.text: Leaving reader put out

indicators.note: 'out' as in a bone out of joint: the letters are knocked from their places

explanation.surface: A reader, put out, walks off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' reads as a phrase meaning annoyed, but 'put' is fodder and only 'out' is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as a noun, 'leaving' is the act of going away, as in 'his leaving was sudden'.

clue.text: Stylish European on stage with a set of books

indicators.note: in a down entry, one thing on another sits above it

parts.note: a leg is a stage of a journey or race
NT = New Testament, a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A chic European performer on stage holding a stack of books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stage' suggests a theatre but means a leg of a journey; the set of books is the New Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: graceful and refined in appearance or manner, as a well-cut suit is.

clue.text: Use bad language about bounds of triple jumper

indicators.note: about means around, so the swearing goes around the letters from triple

parts.note: to swear is to use bad language

indicators.note: the bounds of a word are its edges, so only the first and last letters of triple are used

explanation.surface: An athlete curses over the limits set for the triple jump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumper' looks like the triple jumper in the surface, but it is the garment. 'Bounds of' gives TE from triple, which 'about' puts inside SWEAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Jumper is the British word for a knitted pullover, which is a sweater.

clue.text: Confuse old boy with second course of treatment

parts.note: OB = old boy, a former pupil
a cure is a course of treatment

explanation.surface: An elderly man is bewildered by a second round of medical treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: OB, old boy, is a former pupil of a British school.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to muddy an issue so that nobody can see it clearly.

clue.text: Most excellent drink — remember? Not half!

explanation.surface: A boozy exchange: an excellent drink, remember it? Not half!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for 'absolutely', which disguises the instruction to use only half a word.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: highest in quality or rank, as in a supreme court or effort.

clue.text: In favour of exam? Edward expressed opposition

explanation.surface: Asked whether he backed the exam, Edward objected.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark splits the clue into a dialogue, but the parts simply run on in order.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past tense: objected, spoke out against something.

clue.text: Cook in oven or pan

definitions.meaning: dry-heat cooking of meat or vegetables in an oven
to pan a play is to criticise it harshly

explanation.surface: A recipe choice: cook it in the oven or in a pan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pan' reads as a cooking pot but is the verb for savaging a review, so the kitchen picture hides a second meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Critics who pan a show roast it; cooks roast meat in the oven.

clue.text: Tries displacing river birds

parts.note: a judge hears or tries a case

explanation.surface: Someone attempts to move some water birds off a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tries' is legal: a court tries a case, that is, hears it. Moving its R (river) to the front gives the birds.
explanation.definitionFit: Rheas are large flightless South American birds.

clue.text: Frightening bird protecting rear of nest

indicators.note: the rear of a word is its back end, so only the final letter of nest is taken

explanation.surface: A scary bird guarding the back of its nest.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird is not frightening; 'Frightening' is the definition and the bird is a starling.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: giving a sudden shock or fright.

clue.text: Parisian in bar fight

parts.note: a counter is a bar where drinks are served

explanation.surface: A Frenchman gets into a brawl in a bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container instruction but it is the word a Parisian would say: EN.
explanation.definitionFit: An encounter can be a clash or fight between enemies.

clue.text: Things chaps once put on fish slices

explanation.surface: Men used to put slices of fish on something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put on' reads as placing food on a plate but means wearing: a codpiece was a pouch worn over the groin in Tudor times.
explanation.definitionFit: Codpieces were garments men once wore over their breeches.

clue.text: Pulled in cart at ground with Ted

definitions.note: a past-tense verb: drew towards, as a crowd is drawn in

indicators.note: ground means crushed or milled, so the letters of cart at are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: A cart was hauled into the field, with Ted helping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' looks like a field the cart was pulled into, but it rearranges CART AT into ATTRAC, with TED added after.
explanation.definitionFit: Attracted means drew in, as a magnet or an audience is pulled in by something appealing.

clue.text: Almost everyone bearing weapons is agitated

explanation.surface: Nearly everyone carrying guns is jumpy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' trims one letter from the end of ALL; the surface reads straight, which is why it is easy to miss that 'is' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: worried and flustered, as someone who has had a fright is.

clue.text: Little time before French composer's journeys

indicators.note: 'before' means ahead of, so the time letter is placed ahead of the composer

parts.note: T = time, and a single letter is little
Maurice Ravel was a French composer

explanation.surface: A French composer's trips, just before his time ran short.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s of 'composer’s' is kept as a letter S; Ravel wrote Boléro.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as a plural noun: trips abroad, as in Gulliver's.

clue.text: Ecstasy as golfer oddly gets score of two under par

parts.note: E is slang for the drug ecstasy

indicators.note: take the odd-numbered letters of 'as golfer'

parts.note: A s G o L f E r

explanation.surface: A golfer on drugs plays erratically yet cards a two under par.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' looks like it describes the golfer's play, but it picks letters from both 'as' and 'golfer'.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf an eagle is a hole played two strokes under par.

clue.text: Rubbish clothing wise man first ignored

explanation.surface: A scruffy wise man's clothes are dismissed as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First ignored' reads as the sage being snubbed, but it drops the S at the front of SAGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, the American word for household waste, and also used for nonsense.

clue.text: Non-stop lewdness aroused no wife

indicators.note: aroused means stirred up, so the remaining letters are churned into a new order
no wife means the letter for wife is not present, so it is removed from lewdness

parts.note: W is the standard abbreviation for wife, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: Constant smut stirred up, with the wife no longer around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no wife' takes W out of LEWDNESS, leaving LEDNESS, and 'aroused' stirs those letters into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something endless never finishes, so it carries on without stopping.

clue.text: A piece is cut off

parts.note: a portion or component of a whole

explanation.surface: A slice has been severed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A piece' looks like the subject of the sentence, but it is simply the letters of the answer split in two.
explanation.definitionFit: Something apart is separated, cut off from the rest.

clue.text: Quietly muttered we'd perish at sea

indicators.note: at sea = confused, all over the place

explanation.surface: A sailor murmurs that they would die out on the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At sea' completes a gloomy sailor's line, but means muddled.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: spoke under the breath, so softly that only someone close could hear.

clue.text: Stitch up involving a good salary

indicators.note: involving means containing, so the turned word holds the others
in a down clue up means the letters are read from the bottom

explanation.surface: A worker is framed in a stitch-up over pay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stitch up' reads as framing someone; here SEW goes 'up' to WES, which holds A and G.
explanation.definitionFit: Wages are regular pay for work, a near synonym of salary.

clue.text: Pokes one's nose in cup, perhaps, by the sound of it

indicators.note: by the sound of it means the word is judged as heard, so a word said aloud gives the spelling

parts.note: a cup is an example of a prize, the trophy awarded to a winner

explanation.surface: Someone sticks their nose into a teacup, or so it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cup, perhaps' is a PRIZE, such as a sports trophy; 'by the sound of it' turns that spoken word into its soundalike.
explanation.definitionFit: To pry is to be nosy, so someone who pries interferes inquisitively in other people's business.

clue.text: Observing this writer, for example, pinching money

parts.note: tin is old British slang for money

explanation.surface: A writer is seen stealing some cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinching' reads as stealing money, but it is EG holding TIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Meeting someone is seeing, observing them face to face.

clue.text: Starts to cry loudly, improving friend's mood

indicators.note: the starts of words are their first letters, so one letter is taken from each of the next three words

parts.note: the first letter of each of these three words
a mate is a friend; the 's is read as is, joining the pieces

explanation.surface: A friend's bad temper gets better after they begin to weep noisily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts to' takes the first letters of cry, loudly and improving, CLI, and MATE follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Climate here is the prevailing atmosphere or general feeling, as in a climate of fear, so a mood.

clue.text: Editor turns and notices plans

indicators.note: something that turns faces the other way, so the editor's letters run backwards

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor turns round and spots the schemes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notices' reads as a verb, spots, but is the noun: posted signs.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as a plural noun: drawings or schemes made before building something.

clue.text: Secret agent, with no pressure, checks arrangements

parts.note: to stem a flow is to check it

explanation.surface: A relaxed spy inspects the setup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Checks' reads as inspects, but it means halts, as in stemming a flow.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: organised set-ups, as in a filing or seating arrangement.
